The aurora tonight is a cathedral of vertical emerald curtains rippling left to right, with violet arching between each fold like a living vault, one curtain mid-ripple caught in a long slow wink, a single copper star burning exactly at its hem.

The Milky Way lies overhead as a broad river of gold and blue-white, its own dust lanes splitting it lengthwise into braided channels, and one tiny magenta star sits off the bank like a lantern somebody forgot to collect.

A comet hangs low with a split tail, one arm turquoise and one rose-gold, both sweeping back across a full quarter of the sky, and the hard bright head wears a halo of verdigris that pulses slightly warmer at the centre.

The risen moon is enormous and apricot, flattened, its seas plainly mapped in bronze, the sky around it banding outward from peach to deep saturated violet as though the horizon held its breath and flushed with the effort.

A far storm walls up in magenta towers lit from inside by its own lightning, while directly overhead the sky runs clear indigo crowded with gold, the seam between them sharp and crackling as a ruled line.

The meteor shower is at full pitch, eleven streaks fanning out of one high point in simultaneous white and green, and the deep violet between them holds its stars perfectly still, one streak wider than the rest trailing a brief ember-orange curl at its tip.

The zodiacal light rises as a pale gold cone from the western horizon, impossibly tall and slightly leaning, and every star inside its cone glows warmer than those outside it, one bright teal point sitting just left of the apex like a misplaced jewel.

Noctilucent clouds make electric-blue ribbons very high up, horizontal and perfectly parallel, back-lit by a sun that fell an hour ago, and between two ribbons sits a lone violet star burning steadier than anything that has any right to be that colour.

Two wandering stars hang a finger apart like a pair of lamps, one enormous and cream-gold, the other a smaller apricot bead ringed in one thin bright band, the saturated indigo between them crowded with steady points, the brighter one strong enough to lay a gold path on anything wet.

A star cluster spills thick across one corner of the sky like sugar tipped from a bowl, each grain blue-white or warm gold, and at the cluster's edge one stray member drifts further than the rest as though rolling toward the frame's rim.

The moon in total eclipse has gone deep copper, a whole disc the colour of a cooling coal, sitting inside a ring of clear indigo with two bright emerald stars bracketing it exactly at shoulder distance like appointed guards.

A single enormous fireball crosses the whole sky, leaving a trail of rose-gold that stays for forty seconds, slow-twisting into a helix while the trail's leading edge cools to turquoise and its root still pulses amber over the place it began.

Shells of coloured halo light ring the moon through high ice cloud, innermost rose, then teal, then violet, concentric and slightly oval, and on the outermost ring one gap opens where a thinner patch of cloud has let the indigo through clean.

A red supergiant and a blue-white companion hang side by side, the red one ember-orange and twice the apparent breadth of the blue, and between them a vanishingly thin band of magenta sky reads as though the two stars have coloured their own gap.

The whole sky carries what seems like luminous pollen, a scatter of turquoise motes threading between the gold stars in slow drift, giving every constellation a second nervous outline, and one mote has briefly settled on the Great Bear's spine like a rider.

A wandering planet has visibly moved since the previous night, caught now mid-crossing between a rose star and a gold one, its own amber disc sitting in the gap as though it paused to let the viewer catch up.

The aurora builds into a wall rather than curtains, a solid band of emerald running horizon to horizon at mid-sky, and above it violet deepens through every step to the zenith, the wall's top edge feathering into individual rays that lean back like wheat in wind.

The Milky Way runs diagonal corner to corner as a dense banded river, gold at the core, blue-white at the edges, its dust lanes curling like rivers within a river, and one rose-coloured nebula blushes exactly at the midpoint like a bruise the galaxy earned.

Ice-cloud halos stack four deep around a full moon, rose innermost, then apricot, then turquoise, then the outermost ring going violet and breaking into arcs, and at the top of the outermost arc one extra bright point sits half inside, half out.

Noctilucent cloud stands very high across one whole side of the sky in fine electric-blue ribbons, ripple on ripple of them, lit from beneath in cold silver-violet, and at their far end the ribbons curl back under themselves into one tight bright knot.

The comet's head is a hard turquoise point with a visible green coma and behind it a tail of deep rose splitting into two uneven arms, the longer arm curving gently upward as though the solar wind changed its mind partway through.

The storm's magenta towers have grown to fill the entire eastern horizon now, lightning firing inside each tower in a different rhythm, while the rest of the sky above stays a clean indigo river salted end to end with gold stars unperturbed.

The sky is so crowded with stars that the gaps between them form the pattern, and those gaps run in indigo rivers between islands of gold and blue-white, and one river of gap terminates exactly at a lone ember-orange star as though it aimed there.

Saturn alone hangs in clear violet sky, its rings tilted to maximum, visibly double-banded in apricot and cream, and its largest moon Titan sits to the left at the exact distance that makes the whole arrangement look like an eye with a wayward lash.

Sheets of aurora ripple in emerald and magenta simultaneously, which should be impossible and yet the colours alternate fold by fold across the whole sky, each fold distinct, and at the zenith the two sheets meet and briefly make a white so bright it reads gold.

A copper moon hung deep in eclipse, its whole disc gone the colour of cooling iron, ringed by a thin halo of crushed-violet glass, the surface mottling unevenly — one edge still holding a brighter ember-orange than the rest.

Noctilucent cloud in electric-blue ribbons pulled almost horizontal across the very top of the sky, each ribbon so luminous it throws its own pale wash onto the indigo below, and one ribbon has doubled back and crossed itself into a bright knot.

A dense band of gold and blue-white stars arching shoulder to shoulder overhead, split lengthwise by their own dust lanes so the lanes read as the structure, one solitary rose-coloured star burning steady well outside the main crowd.

A far storm walled up along one horizon in towers lit magenta from inside by its own lightning, while directly overhead the sky holds clear saturated indigo, both weathers meeting at a hard seam that flickers every few seconds.

A comet sitting low with a split tail, one arm pale green and one arm dusty rose, the two leaning apart across a quarter of the sky, the head wrapped in a tight turquoise haze sharper than anything else in the frame.

A wandering star caught mid-crossing between two brighter companions, visibly displaced from where it stood the night before, the three forming an uneven emerald-and-gold triangle that was a straight line just yesterday.

A meteor shower at its absolute peak, eleven streaks all leaning out of one high point at once, the trails white and green, the deep violet between them so crowded with steady stars the streaks look threaded through fabric.

A full ring of coloured halo light around a high moon, the inner edge a warm apricot grading outward through turquoise, the whole ring perfectly circular except one short arc that widens as though the ice cloud thickened there for a moment.

The pale cone of zodiacal light standing straight up from the horizon where the sun has gone, a clean triangle of gold dust rising through violet sky, and at its very tip a single blue-white star sits exactly centred, as though placed.

An aurora in tall vertical curtains from horizon to zenith, the hem a committed emerald so vivid it looks woven, the upper reach bleeding into violet, one whole curtain folded double and pulsing brighter than the rest in slow rhythmic surges.

A sky so impossibly thick with stars that the gaps between them form the pattern — a lace of indigo holes in a cloth of gold, and off to one side a tight cluster spilled like split sugar from a pouch still mid-pour.

A huge apricot moon just risen and still slightly flattened at the base, tangled in the upper branches, its seas clearly visible as warm umber patches, the sky around it grading outward through peach into saturated violet.

A cluster of several hundred stars packed so tightly they blur at the centre into a single gold smear, the edges resolving into turquoise individual points, and on close inspection one of the outermost stars has a faint ember companion pressed against its side.

Two bright wandering stars a finger's width apart, one distinctly amber and one distinctly blue-white, close enough to share a faint aureole of diffracted light between them, the surrounding indigo giving each one a coloured shadow it ought to have earned.

The whole sky slowly drifting with luminous gold pollen, each mote independent and moving at a slightly different pace, so the background stars have warm company and the constellations are temporarily stranger, their lines connected by new floating points.

A long slow fireball crossing the full width of the sky, leaving a rose-and-amber trail that holds its shape and does not dissipate, the trail slowly twisting into a shallow corkscrew as the high winds work it, still glowing a full minute on.

Shells of colour around the moon through a veil of ice cloud — innermost ring apricot, next ring turquoise, outermost ring a thin violet — the shells not quite concentric, all shifted slightly left so the moon sits off-centre in its own target.

A green-and-magenta aurora that has formed a single great arc rather than curtains, one enormous bow from east to west, its top so high it seems to belong to a different part of the atmosphere, the green edge shivering while the magenta holds still.

A satellite catching sunlight below the terminator and crossing the zenith at a steady pace, blazing amber against the indigo sky, followed at an exact interval by a second one, the pair crossing like a slow deliberately placed pair of stitches.

A storm cloud anvil lit from inside by lightning in gold-and-violet pulses, the top of the anvil itself catching the last of some other light and going a deep rose, while through a clear gap at the side the ordinary stars continue burning indigo.

A moon in a ring of ice-crystal colour where the halo has developed a bright spot — a mock moon — sitting exactly ninety degrees to the right, equally apricot, equally sharp, so the sky briefly holds two credible moons on the same ring.

The Milky Way running as a dense banded arch of blue-white overhead, split by dust lanes, with a warm rose nebula visible to anyone looking for thirty seconds at one specific mid-point, so faint it seems to blink in and out like an ember.

Noctilucent cloud in overlapping waves of electric blue and silver-violet, the waves running in opposite directions and interfering into a bright grid at the centre, the highest and brightest node sitting precisely at the zenith like a lamp someone remembered to leave on.

A comet's head showing a clear turquoise coma with a single vivid green jet curving back into the main tail, the tail itself broad and gold and fanning outward, the whole structure sitting just above the treeline in a sky of deepest violet.

A sky event as rare as a second sunrise — a bright wandering star with visible amber colour crossing in front of a tight cluster, threading through the group like a bead on a wire, the cluster's turquoise stars crowding close around it on all sides.

An aurora unlike curtains — a single rotating oval of light directly overhead as if the sky has an eye, the iris emerald and the pupil going deep violet at the centre, slowly turning clockwise, a structure people will argue about for days after.

A dense asteroid stream arriving in slow threes and fours rather than a shower, the streaks emerald with violet afterburns, each trailing long enough to overlap the next, so at peak the frame holds nine parallel glowing lines all slightly displaced from one another.

A ring of luminous rose-gold light around a star too bright to be ordinary, the ring a perfect tight circle suggesting ice cloud directly in front, and just inside the ring on the left a tiny turquoise companion star sits embedded in the glow.

The zodiacal band fully visible as a faint gold belt running the full width of the sky coast to coast, crossing the overhead star-river at a steep angle, the intersection point visibly brighter where the two structures of light reinforce each other into apricot.

An aurora so low and wide it fills the lower third of the sky like a hem of gathered cloth, vivid emerald at the base folding into deep violet as it rises, one heavy pleat catching its own light and glowing brighter than adjacent folds.

A copper moon in full eclipse, swollen and round, its whole disc gone the colour of a cooling ember, rings of apricot and deep rose spreading outward through ice crystal into the indigo around it, one tiny wandering star caught inside the outermost ring like a bead in a groove.

The zodiacal cone standing straight up from the horizon where the sun drowned, a solid triangle of gold dust narrowing to a needle point, the surrounding sky a saturated violet that makes the cone seem lit from inside, a lone bright wanderer sitting exactly on the cone's central axis.

A noctilucent display running in electric-blue ribbons very high up, crossing and recurving like folded silk, the colour so charged it reads closer to turquoise against the deep rose that still clings to the upper atmosphere, the lowest ribbon fraying at one tip into threads fine as spun sugar.

A comet low with a split tail, one arm green as a lamp through bottle-glass and one arm rose-gold, the two diverging across a quarter of the sky while the head burns as a hard turquoise point, the rose arm faintly braided where it thins toward the edge.

A meteor shower pouring out of one point overhead, eleven streaks crossing at once in gold and cold blue-white, all leaning in the same direction like thrown glass threads, the violet sky between them unchanged and crowded, one streak ending in a brief bright flare instead of fading.

A full aurora wall, emerald curtains running north to south, their hems rippling as though a hand moved behind cloth, violet climbing from the emerald tops straight up into indigo, one single fold brighter than the rest and holding its brightness while all the others pulse and shift.

A dense star cluster spilled thick across one quarter of the sky, gold and blue-white packed so close the spaces between them are the pattern, a ring of slightly redder stars circling the cluster's edge, one amber point sitting just outside the ring as though it rolled free.

A pair of wandering stars a finger apart, one apricot and one blue-white, each one steady where the surrounding stars shimmer, the sky between them a saturated indigo through which smaller stars crowd without touching, the apricot one visibly lower than last night, caught mid-crossing.

A far storm walled up in towers of cloud along one edge of the sky, every tower lit magenta from inside by its own lightning, the overhead sky staying clear and violet, crowded with gold stars, the boundary between storm-wall and starfield a single hard luminous seam.

The Milky Way as a dense band running corner to corner, gold and blue-white split lengthwise by its own dust lanes, the lanes so deep in colour they read as violet ribbons drawn through the gold, a small rose star burning alone on the band's near edge.

A halo ringing the moon, three shells of colour nested inside each other, innermost a warm apricot, the next ring going turquoise, the outermost dissolving into rose where it meets the deep indigo sky, a single fixed bright star sitting exactly on the turquoise ring.

A wandering star caught mid-crossing between two bright fixed ones, forming a tight triangle tonight that did not exist yesterday, its colour a warmer amber against the blue-white of its neighbours, the whole trio sitting in an otherwise sparse violet field that makes the grouping easy to read.

A sky so saturated with stars that the gaps between them form the pattern, the violet background barely showing through the gold and blue-white crowd, one small area of slightly thicker sky near the top reading as a dark lane until a very slow satellite threads through it.

A one-star meteor, enormous, crossing the whole sky in five slow seconds and leaving a rose and gold trail that stays lit for a full breath after the head is gone, the trail bending very slightly where it crossed into warmer air, then fading from rose to apricot before it closes.

Noctilucent cloud in turquoise sheets folded into one another very high and lit from inside, the folds casting faint shadows on the sheets behind them, the sky beneath them deep indigo and clear, one early meteor threading through the lower indigo and lighting the turquoise above it briefly from below.

A crowded cluster of seven stars in a tight group, each one a slightly different warmth, ranging from gold to blue-white, surrounded by a sparse indigo field that makes the group seem pressed together, a faint rose haze filling the space between the innermost four like caught breath.

An aurora that has spread to fill the whole overhead, emerald at the zenith shifting to violet at every horizon, no curtains now but a single shimmering dome, one bright wandering star showing through the emerald centre as though the light were glass and not air.

A moon just risen, huge and apricot, flattened at its base by the thick air it has barely cleared, its seas showing as smudged violet-grey against the warm surface, the sky immediately around it going peach then rose then the deep indigo that holds all the overhead stars.

A slow luminous rain of pollen-light across the whole sky, gold motes drifting among the fixed stars and giving each one a small companion of light, a swarm of wandering sparks moving steadily in one direction at the same speed, the background indigo thickening between them to deep violet.

A comet sitting high tonight, higher than last week, its green head hard and bright with a turquoise haze dissolving into indigo around it, the single tail sweeping back in apricot-tinged gold, the tail's outer edge braided into three distinct threads that refuse to merge.

A storm building on the right side of the sky, its cloud towers lit from inside by gold and magenta lightning in two colours at once, the left side clear and indigo and carrying a dense band of stars, the seam between them a perfect vertical line.

A moon so high it has shrunk to a small hard disc but carries a triple halo, the innermost ring pure rose, the second turquoise, the third the faintest apricot before the deep indigo takes over, a wandering star sitting exactly on the turquoise ring.

A satellite swarm rising in a slow curved arc, a firefly procession of gold points evenly spaced, curving up out of the indigo horizon and dimming one by one as they climb into full sun, the last four still bright and the first six already gone to embers.

The zodiacal band running edge to edge, a broad gold and rose avenue of light wider than a fist held up, the indigo above and below it pressing in so the band seems to glow from inside, a lone blue-white star sitting precisely on the band's centreline.

An aurora low on the horizon only, a single curtain of emerald that stays flat rather than rising, its top edge fraying into violet threads that climb a little before dissolving into indigo, one fold of the curtain brighter than the rest and pulsing at a different rhythm.

A full spectrum halo around the moon through ice cloud, the innermost ring apricot shading to gold, then a gap of clear indigo, then a second larger ring of rose and turquoise running together, the whole assembly perfectly centred, one star caught between the two rings.

A dense star field where the stars crowd so thick the eye reads the gold clusters as positive shapes and the indigo gaps as the negative space, a slow satellite threading through without touching a single star, leaving a straight ruled line of motion across the crowded field.

A meteor shower at peak, eight streaks in the frame at once, four in white-gold and four in cold green-blue, all leaning back from one bright point like cracked glass spreading from an impact, the violet field between them unchanged, one streak ending with a visible burst.

A far storm walled tall on the left, its towers lit in rose and apricot from inside, the right side of the sky staying clear indigo, a crowd of gold stars overhead, the storm wall casting an apricot reflection upward into the clear air above its own clouds.

A zodiacal cone standing at midsummer steepness, nearly vertical, a solid column of gold dust against a deep violet sky, the column narrowing to a hair at the top, a single apricot wandering star sitting inside the cone a third of the way up, slightly brighter than the dust around it.

The zodiacal cone stands straight up from the horizon like a pillar of frosted glass, its gold spine thickening toward the base and its edges dissolving into violet, a single wandering star caught mid-drift exactly inside its narrowest tip.

An eclipse moon hung high and swollen in full copper, its face crossed by one long ember-orange streak where a meteor has just burned through the same patch of sky, the copper and the orange refusing to agree on which is brighter.

Noctilucent ribbons braided electric-blue very high above everything else, looping in slow cold arcs like frost drawn on the inside of a glass dome, one ribbon kinked where it meets a crowded cluster and seems, absurdly, to go around it.

A star cluster spilled thick as sugar granules across a quarter of the sky, each grain returning light in either gold or blue-white so the patch reads as two overlapping clouds, a lone rose-coloured point standing apart like a bead rolled free.

The aurora tonight hangs in a single enormous curtain of emerald, not rippling but rigid, as though starched — then one vertical fold releases and swings through magenta before going still again, the rest of the curtain pretending nothing happened.

A comet sitting at a low angle with its twin tails peeled apart, one arm green as bottle glass and one a warm apricot, both spanning nearly half the sky, its nucleus a hard turquoise bead trailing a short haze of its own.

The whole sky carrying luminous pollen — a copper-gold drift so even and fine it seems to be falling upward, each mote slower than a snowflake, while beneath it the true stars burn through in saturated violet and refuse to be softened.

A far storm walled along the left quarter in towers of cloud, each tower lit magenta from its interior by its own lightning, while the right three-quarters holds clear deep indigo and steady gold stars, both weathers sharing one hard luminous seam.

A moon still low and enormous, flattened and apricot-orange, its seas showing as grey-violet bruises across its face, the sky immediately around it going peach then rose then a deep singing indigo that crowds in from all sides.

Two bright wanderers hanging a finger-width apart like a pair of lanterns someone forgot, one gold and one blue-white, their combined light strong enough to cast a faint cone of illumination upward into the indigo above them, paling it to teal.

A meteor shower with eleven or twelve streaks crossing at once, all leaning out of one high point, each streak briefly emerald at its tip and white along its length, the deep violet sky between them absolutely still and packed with ordinary stars.

Shells of colour ringing the moon through ice cloud — innermost ring a hot rose-gold, middle ring turquoise, outermost ring violet, each circle crisp as a blown glass rim, the moon herself the one cold white thing at the centre of all that warmth.

The Milky Way as a dense broad band of gold and blue-white running shoulder to shoulder across the whole sky, its dust lanes reading as the deliberate pattern, one small red star burning alone on the lower edge like an ember set aside to cool.

A ring of firefly-bright satellites moving in a line low across the sky, each one amber, evenly spaced, rising in formation toward a crowded cluster as though they have an appointment, the blue-violet sky between each pair perfectly matched.

One enormous falling star crossing slowly, slowly — a traveller rather than a dart — trailing a persisting violet ribbon that holds its curve for ten seconds after the gold head has gone, the ribbon brightening rather than fading, then snapping out entirely.
